title: Raised fields in the Titicaca basin: ancient use and modern rehabilitation
period: Ancient local use from approximately three millennia before 1992; separate rehabilitation episode, 1980s–2000
summary: Raised fields altered water and crop microclimates. Ancient archaeological persistence and modern reconstructed-plot results do not prove universal labour superiority or durable revival; complete rotations and local institutions change the comparison.

stages.invention: No precise invention or single origin assigned. Erickson's local chronology indicates early use roughly three millennia before his 1992 study.
stages.feasibility: Twentieth-century experimental blocks demonstrate operating configurations and local thermal effects; ancient conditions are inferred rather than reproduced exactly.
stages.deployment: Archaeological earthworks and rebuilding establish ancient deployment; promoted projects rebuilt fields from the 1980s.
stages.diffusion: Neither ancient simultaneous area nor modern participating-household share is established here. Reconstruction totals are not a denominator of sustained use.
stages.scaling: A productive experimental plot does not measure complete-rotation labour, maintenance or organisation across a landscape.
stages.non-adoption: Bandy reports disappointing persistence in specified revived fields, alongside other continuing reconstruction.
stages.displacement: Ancient disuse and twentieth-century project abandonment are separate events. No single climatic, political or labour explanation is assigned to both.

counterevidence: Some raised-field comparisons are favourable and communities differ. Bandy's critique inherits earlier measurements and does not supply a basin-wide abandonment census or prove ancient farmers inefficient.

episode.technology_configuration: A: ancient elevated planting platforms with intervening canals, varying locally. B: experimental and promoted reconstructions beginning in the 1980s, with modern crops, labour and project support.
episode.task: Produce crops in a high-altitude lakeshore environment while managing water, frost exposure and seasonal labour; the relative importance of these goals is contested.
episode.population: A: cultivators inferred from northern-basin archaeology; no enumerated ancient population. B: experimental blocks and named rehabilitation programmes reviewed by Erickson and Bandy; Swartley's revisited fields are a limited subset.
episode.interval: A: long ancient sequence, with early local use approximately three millennia before 1992 and no uniform basin-wide endpoints. B: research/revival from the 1980s, revisits in 1996–1997 and reconstruction reports through 2000.
contemporary_alternatives: Dryland potato cultivation and rotations with fallow
Other water/land management suited to local sites
Modern households' alternative crops and livelihoods; exact menus vary and are incompletely observed
episode.adoption_measure: A: surviving field morphology and excavated rebuilding are deployment proxies, not a diffusion rate. B: local reports of reconstruction and cessation; no common denominator of sustained users or maintained area.
episode.observation_limits: Preservation and dated excavation are uneven; experimental blocks are small. Modern labour comparisons use heterogeneous studies; important programme originals were not acquired. The subepisodes cannot be treated as one longitudinal experiment.

actors.chooser: A: ancient household/community/elite decision authority remains uncertain. B: project promoters and cultivators both shape construction and continued cultivation; their decisions need not share objectives.
actors.payer: A: labour and resource contributions are archaeologically uncertain. B: projects supply some resources while participating cultivators bear labour and maintenance; precise subsidy incidence differs by programme and is not fully reconstructed.
actors.operator_maintainer: Cultivators build/repair platforms and canals and perform cropping. Ancient division of work and modern paid versus unpaid shares are not adequately measured.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Household members and neighbours sharing land, water and labour demands; their individual consent and benefits are not recoverable from the main measures.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Ancient compulsion versus voluntary cooperation is unresolved. Modern cessation demonstrates an ability to cease use in observed projects, but does not reveal every participant's constraints or all entry conditions.

labour.tasks: Earthmoving, canal/platform maintenance and crop work; a larger initial harvest may involve more construction or recurring work than the dryland comparator.
labour.entry_barriers: Access to suitable land/water, labour at the required season and local agronomic/maintenance knowledge; programme access adds a modern institutional barrier.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Ancient control and political mobilisation are disputed. Modern project totals do not identify who owns improvements or captures each household member's return.
labour.transition: Bandy reviews revival and later cessations; no complete person-level livelihood trajectory or common duration-to-exit distribution is available.
labour.distribution: Per-hectare and per-workday outcomes can rank systems differently. Gender, status and household distributions are insufficiently observed for aggregate claims.
labour.evidence_limit: Experimental yields and schematic labour accounting do not estimate employment creation, wage effects or welfare for ancient or modern populations.

title: Balinese subak calendars: irrigation coordination and recombination with modern rice
period: 1970s–1980s intervention history; directly described crop calendar, 1988–1989; later model reanalysis
summary: Shared water and pest ecology make rice calendars interdependent. The observed system combines coordinated calendars with modern varieties, while independent model reanalysis limits claims of universal synchronisation or institutional optimality.

stages.invention: Neither irrigation nor water-temple institutional origin is identified by the modern observations/model.
stages.feasibility: Operating canals, calendars and rice varieties are observed; model performance is conditional on ecology and decision rules.
stages.deployment: The 172-subak model covers a specified two-river system; a 1988–1989 Manuaba calendar uses coordinated timing and named improved varieties.
stages.diffusion: No Bali-wide denominator or independent diffusion curve is reconstructed. National programme history is accessed through scholarly accounts.
stages.scaling: Watershed coordination concerns interactions beyond individual plots, but optimal coordination size and distribution are model-dependent.
stages.non-adoption: Failure to follow individually intensified schedules can reflect water/pest interactions, not inability to use modern seed.
stages.displacement: Restored calendar coordination coexists with modern varieties rather than wholesale technological reversal.

counterevidence: Janssen reproduces central results under original assumptions but changes them under other plausible rules. Historical intervention narratives are not independently corroborated by a second field experiment.

episode.technology_configuration: Canal irrigation, rice varieties and subak/temple-linked planting/fallow calendars in the Oos–Petanu setting; model variants are analytically distinct from measured practice.
episode.task: Grow rice while allocating water and limiting pest habitat across interconnected fields.
episode.population: 172 subaks represented in the model and local crop/water observations; the reported Manuaba calendar is a specific observed configuration, not every Balinese farmer.
episode.interval: Intervention/disruption and restoration narratives cover the 1970s–1980s; directly described calendar is 1988–1989. The 1993 model and 2006 proof/2007 reanalysis are evidence dates, not new diffusion intervals.
contemporary_alternatives: Independent intensified planting schedules
Synchronised fallow and planting
Coordinated staggered schedules where water scarcity warrants them
Different local rice-variety mixes
episode.adoption_measure: Qualitative records of calendars, named varieties and coordination; simulated yields under alternative schedules. No common measured household adoption share.
episode.observation_limits: Simulation outputs must not be counted as field outcomes. Model reanalysis shares underlying ecology/data and inherited history; original programme memoranda were not acquired.

actors.chooser: Individual farmers, subak groups, temple-linked coordinators and national agricultural programmes operate at different decision scales.
actors.payer: Farmers contribute cultivation and irrigation resources; state programmes support promoted packages. Complete financial and labour incidence is not reconstructed.
actors.operator_maintainer: Farmers and irrigation associations implement calendars and water management; the inspected sources do not quantify every paid/unpaid maintenance contribution.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Upstream/downstream farmers and neighbours exposed to pests/water demand are affected by choices elsewhere; their gains can differ.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Accounts describe programme pressure and farmer restoration of coordination. The evidence does not measure each farmer's sanctions, exit options or consent to every calendar.

labour.tasks: Crop timing, canal/water management, communication and collective decisions reorganise farming work; yield optimisation can change workload and water access differently by subak.
labour.entry_barriers: Land/water access, local irrigation knowledge and institutional participation; institutional authority is not directly measured as a credential or wage premium.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Water and timing decisions are interdependent; aggregate simulated harvest does not identify how bargaining distributes gains among associations or farmers.
labour.transition: Historical restoration/recombination is described, but no individual worker panel traces job loss, earnings or career transition.
labour.distribution: Janssen shows that maximising watershed output and distributing gains evenly are different objectives; person-level livelihood gains remain unmeasured.
labour.evidence_limit: Ecological models cannot establish universal worker welfare, consent or the historical cause of institutional formation.

title: Jahaly-Pacharr irrigation: rice output, rights and labour in The Gambia
period: 1984–1990 project use, with prior-rights context and 1983–1984 fieldwork
summary: A technical and credit package expanded rice opportunities, while project land reclassification and household authority altered who controlled returns. Early income benefits coexist with crop substitution, uneven individual incentives and later operating problems.

stages.invention: The project deploys existing pumps, land preparation, improved rice and credit; it is not an invention-priority case.
stages.feasibility: Irrigated rice production is demonstrated, conditional on water control, inputs, machinery and labour calendars.
stages.deployment: Project participants cultivate irrigated plots from 1984; fieldwork/evaluation describes households and farmers in participating and comparison villages.
stages.diffusion: No complete regional participation/time-series denominator is reconstructed. Nominal registration is not control or actual labour supplied.
stages.scaling: Continued operations involve fuel, parts, input prices, credit and marketing alongside labour mobilisation.
stages.non-adoption: Some women with alternatives resist uncompensated obligations or negotiate wages/shares; low utilisation can also reflect competing rainfed returns.
stages.displacement: Labour shifts between irrigated and other crops and toward paid groups; no simple complete replacement of older rice systems is established.

counterevidence: IFPRI reports substantial early production/income benefits; Carney's later problems do not erase them. Neither observational design fully separates project selection, rights, operational failures and reallocation.

episode.technology_configuration: Pumped irrigation, water control, mechanical land preparation, short-duration rice, purchased inputs, credit and prescribed cultivation schedules, embedded in local household/land institutions.
episode.task: Raise rice output and income; women and household heads may separately seek control over crop returns and labour time.
episode.population: Carney's fieldwork and follow-ups in project communities, and IFPRI's 200-household/about-900-farmer survey in ten villages. These are related project populations but not a reconciled panel of identical people and years.
episode.interval: Early 1984–1986 evaluation and field follow-ups through 1990, with pre-project cultivation-rights context.
contemporary_alternatives: Existing swamp, tidal and rainfed rice
Upland crops and independently controlled plots
Paid labour groups or negotiated family labour
Different seasonal allocation when rainfall is favourable
episode.adoption_measure: Project access, plot/crop production, labour participation and qualitative rights/control reports. Plot registration is not effective ownership; yields alone are not household welfare.
episode.observation_limits: Largely observational comparisons with different study dates and purposes; Carney cites some IFPRI results, so all findings are not independent corroboration. Input/price/repair changes overlap rights conflicts.

actors.chooser: Donors and project managers choose the package/schedules; household heads, women cultivators and labour groups negotiate or contest land and work decisions. Project management controls continued plot access through production-credit rules and sanctions.
actors.payer: Donor/project resources and credit support infrastructure/inputs; cultivators and households bear repayment, labour and operating costs, distributed unevenly.
actors.operator_maintainer: Women perform much rice work alongside household/project labour arrangements; machinery/pumps require operating and repair personnel. Paid groups coexist with uncompensated family obligations.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Women without matching crop control, other household workers, children affected by care/nutrition, and producers whose other crops lose labour.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Project credit contracts put continued usufruct at risk after repayment failure. Carney reports 1990 plot seizures and negotiated conditional return after debt repayment (AGR-K25). Separately, women negotiated, withdrew labour or formed paid groups where outside plots/political connections permitted; others faced household obligations and weak alternatives. These interacting constraints do not make every workday coerced or registration proof of consent.

labour.tasks: Rice preparation, planting, weeding and harvesting are reorganised around tighter water/crop schedules; women adapt groups toward paid work, and other crops lose labour.
labour.entry_barriers: Access to irrigated plots, credit, inputs and local authority; independent upland rights and political connections shape alternatives and bargaining.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Reclassification can transfer control to household heads despite women being registered. Wages, crop shares and independent plots alter who captures returns. Project management could seize plots for repayment arrears; the 1990 compromise preserved conditional reclamation. This contract power is distinct from household control of proceeds.
labour.transition: Fieldwork spans initial rollout and later follow-ups through 1990; it is not a complete worker panel or estimate of time needed to replace lost income.
labour.distribution: Household income gains can coincide with weaker individual control and greater maternal work burdens. Ethnic/community and household contrasts matter; averages do not identify each woman's gain.
labour.evidence_limit: No credible single percentage of project decline is assigned to labour resistance, and household totals cannot establish individual welfare or consent.

title: Modern crop varieties, 1965–2010, and a bounded Indian groundwater contrast
period: Variety effects, 1965–2010; distinct groundwater observation, August 2002–October 2008
outcome: large measured yield contribution under model assumptions
summary: Modern varieties spread with local adaptation and supporting systems. An econometric study estimates large direct yield gains, while a separately measured Indian groundwater episode demonstrates why output alone cannot describe resource costs or identify their exact technological cause.

stages.invention: Crop breeding and release are plural processes; no single invention date is assigned to the whole Green Revolution.
stages.feasibility: Varieties' realised performance depends on crop, environment, adaptation and inputs; shorter maturity can alter multiple-cropping possibilities.
stages.deployment: Release/adoption data cover food crops and countries in the specified research sample; regional Indian pumping is a different observed system.
stages.diffusion: Historical country/crop adoption and release variation enter the Gollin study; no universal farmer-level adoption percentage is asserted here.
stages.scaling: The direct yield estimate holds allocations fixed; reallocation and wider economic effects are distinct model components.
stages.non-adoption: Lower uptake in marginal environments may reflect unsuitable complements, risk or access; it does not uniquely identify reluctance or ignorance.
stages.displacement: New varieties and altered crop choices can coexist with older cultivars; this contribution does not reconstruct complete variety replacement or biodiversity loss.

counterevidence: Large average yield estimates do not imply universal gains. Resource depletion is measured in a particular region and period and is not an identified seed-specific effect; different studies share some underlying crop-data traditions.

episode.technology_configuration: A: modern food-crop varieties with locally varying breeding, irrigation and input systems. B: northwestern Indian groundwater extraction within a farming/water-use system, independently measured rather than assigned as an effect of a particular seed.
episode.task: A: increase crop yield and feasible production. B: provide water for irrigation and other uses while the study measures changes in groundwater stock.
episode.population: A: crop-country observations and a 90-country baseline in Gollin et al., with broader retrospective context from Pingali. B: regional storage across Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana including Delhi; a geographic stock measure, not the same people as the yield sample.
episode.interval: A: 1965–2010. B: August 2002–October 2008. These are linked conceptually for accounting, not a matched causal comparison.
contemporary_alternatives: Existing locally adapted varieties and crop mixes
Alternative breeding/innovation paths excluded from the strict no-modern-varieties counterfactual
Rainfed or differently irrigated production where feasible
Different water-use/crop choices, not assumed equally accessible
episode.adoption_measure: A: historical modern-variety/release variation and modelled yield contribution, not an ownership census. B: satellite-derived groundwater stock trend; no adoption measure and no seed attribution.
episode.observation_limits: Country/crop aggregation obscures household distribution. Release timing needs identification assumptions; the groundwater estimate uses modelled storage subtraction. Domains, denominators and intervals differ.

actors.chooser: Breeders, national research programmes, public agencies and farmers choose different parts of the system; pumping/crop decisions and water policy need not be made by the same actors.
actors.payer: Public/international research and local infrastructure finance coexist with farmer input expenditure. Costs and subsidies vary; exact incidence is not reconstructed across the sample.
actors.operator_maintainer: Farmers, workers, irrigation/pump operators and input/service suppliers sustain use; breeding requires continuing research and adaptation.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Consumers affected by food supply/prices, landless labourers, households with unequal access, downstream or future groundwater users; their effects are not all measured by the selected studies.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Farmer adoption choices are observed under constrained land, water, price and policy conditions. These data do not establish free choice for every worker or allow future water users to refuse depletion.

labour.tasks: Changes in cropping frequency, input application, irrigation and crop allocation can reorganise work; the contribution does not estimate a uniform labour-saving or labour-using effect.
labour.entry_barriers: Locally suitable seed, water, knowledge, finance, land and input access; relative importance varies by crop and environment.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Land/water ownership and input/price policy can affect capture of productivity gains, but the selected aggregate yield estimate does not identify individual bargaining outcomes.
labour.transition: The crop-country series spans decades, not individual occupational transitions; resource monitoring spans six years and does not trace household adjustment.
labour.distribution: Average yield gains are not a measure of who gained income or control. Groundwater losses impose potential costs beyond current extracting households; exact household incidence is unmeasured here.
labour.evidence_limit: No individual employment forecast, universal farmer welfare claim or seed-specific depletion share follows from these studies.

title: Fallow investment and practical land security in Akwapim, Ghana
period: Late twentieth-century two-year survey; exact calendar dates not established in inspected description
summary: Fallowing is an investment through waiting. Plot histories and within-household/cultivator contrasts connect practical security, political position and fallow decisions, while leaving causal exclusion restrictions and the best remedy open.

stages.invention: No invention date is relevant or inferred; fallowing is an existing practice.
stages.feasibility: Soil recovery requires leaving land unused for a period, with subsequent access sufficiently secure to capture returns.
stages.deployment: The survey observes cultivation and fallow histories in four Akwapim clusters.
stages.diffusion: The study compares investment intensity/security, not national spread of a purchased device or a new practice.
stages.scaling: More investment may require land/time security rather than simply supplying equipment or knowledge; no scale-up programme is evaluated.
stages.non-adoption: Shorter fallow can be a response to expropriation risk or other constraints, not a failure to understand agronomy.
stages.displacement: Earlier recultivation is the relevant competing practice; no wholesale historical displacement trajectory is reconstructed.

counterevidence: Political status may carry wealth, labour and other advantages. Within-person/plot-provenance contrasts address some rivals but do not randomly assign power or establish formal title as the only solution.

episode.technology_configuration: Fallow–cultivation rotations under locally negotiated land-control arrangements; waiting is the productive investment.
episode.task: Restore soil productivity while retaining the ability to return and harvest the investment's payoff.
episode.population: Cultivators and plots in Goldstein and Udry's repeated survey of four Akwapim village clusters; not all Ghanaian farmers and not the northern Ghana insurance sample.
episode.interval: Two-year survey with retrospective plot histories, late twentieth century; the inspected survey description does not fix calendar endpoints.
contemporary_alternatives: Cultivate again sooner to maintain a claim
Longer fallow where control is secure
Other soil-improvement inputs, whose equivalent feasibility is not established by this case
episode.adoption_measure: Fallow duration, plot use, tenure/political position and estimated agricultural returns; no binary new-technology adoption share.
episode.observation_limits: Observational and instrumental-variable identification relies on restrictions. Plot histories and practical security are imperfect; a legal document and effective control are distinct.

actors.chooser: Individual cultivators choose timing subject to household, lineage and local authority over land; choices can differ within the same household.
actors.payer: Cultivators bear foregone current production and risk of losing access; no purchased-equipment payer is required for the central investment.
actors.operator_maintainer: Cultivators manage the rotation and later crop work. Waiting may reduce current plot labour while imposing a longer return horizon.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Household members dependent on output and people with competing claims to land; gendered authority changes who can retain control.
actors.ability_to_refuse: A farmer can shorten fallow but may not be able to secure the land through waiting. Women generally have less local political power in the study; formal legal freedom does not establish equal feasible options.

labour.tasks: Cultivation is rescheduled over longer or shorter rotations; the central choice is land/time allocation, not an observed new occupation.
labour.entry_barriers: Secure practical access to land and local political standing; foregone current output can matter alongside cash and agronomic knowledge.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Control during non-use affects who captures delayed productivity gains; a household-level owner label can hide distinct cultivator rights.
labour.transition: Repeated observation and plot histories identify investment patterns, not a worker reskilling or occupational-transition sequence.
labour.distribution: Women are less often politically powerful and face shorter effective investment horizons. Estimates do not prove all gender differences arise through one channel.
labour.evidence_limit: No universal effect of titling, no comparison of every soil technology, and no causal national gender-welfare estimate.

title: Rainfall insurance and investment choices in northern Ghana
summary: Randomised cash and insurance treatments distinguish constraints more directly than stated obstacles alone. Insurance changes production choices, while demand for the insurance itself and the welfare consequences of greater investment remain separate questions.

stages.invention: The study tests specific rainfall-index contracts, not priority for agricultural insurance.
stages.feasibility: Weather-index triggers, delivery and payout systems operate within the experiment; basis risk is inherent to the tested matching of index and individual loss.
stages.deployment: Sampled farmers receive grants or offers under randomised treatment conditions and varying prices.
stages.diffusion: Experimental purchase/renewal responses are measured over three years; they do not establish sustained full-cost commercial diffusion.
stages.scaling: Delivery cost, insurer viability, index accuracy and credible payment remain untested requirements for a broader market claim.
stages.non-adoption: Declining an offer can reflect price, basis risk, beliefs or liquidity timing; payout-sensitive demand does not uniquely identify a psychological bias.
stages.displacement: Production choices shift with risk protection, but the study does not establish complete replacement of existing risk-management practices.

counterevidence: Insurance and cash treatments differ in value/timing/state contingency. Investment effects do not establish net profit or welfare gains; local causal results cannot show credit never constrains farmers elsewhere.

episode.technology_configuration: Rainfall-index crop insurance, cash grants and randomised offers/prices for sampled farmers, with agricultural expenditure and production measured across seasons.
episode.task: Manage catastrophic rainfall risk and decide how much and how riskily to invest in farming.
episode.population: Sampled northern Ghana maize farmers in Karlan et al.'s 2009–2011 experiments; not the Akwapim tenure sample and not a representative census of African farmers.
episode.interval: Three agricultural seasons, 2009–2011, including grant and purchase opportunities.
contemporary_alternatives: Cash support without insurance
Lower-risk or lower-input production
Existing household/network coping and resource mobilisation
Declining the offered contract
episode.adoption_measure: Experimental insurance offers/purchases, response to randomised prices and reported agricultural investment; treatment-assignment denominators are study-specific, not regional penetration.
episode.observation_limits: The causal offer effect is stronger than psychological interpretations of payout/network correlations. Cost-complete commercial renewal and wider welfare are not established.

actors.chooser: Researchers/insurers define treatment offers; farmers choose investment and, where offered, whether/how much insurance to purchase.
actors.payer: Experiment-funded grants/subsidies and farmers paying offered premiums; full commercial delivery incidence is not evaluated.
actors.operator_maintainer: Farmers operate farms; insurers and programme staff maintain index, contract and payment delivery. Contract credibility depends on those institutions.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Household members and workers share production risk and expenditure consequences; their individual consent and gains are not isolated by farm-level responses.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Purchase offers can be declined and price response is observed. Constraints and household authority still shape choices; receipt of a grant is not evidence of willingness to pay its full cost.

labour.tasks: Investment and production choices change; the paper's causal result is not a universal labour-displacement estimate or new-job count.
labour.entry_barriers: Premium price, contract understanding, index–loss fit, payment credibility and delivery access; cash alone does not remove every constraint.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Farm decision-makers allocate supported resources, but intra-household control of gains and losses is not fully identified.
labour.transition: Three seasons capture learning/demand changes but do not track long occupational transitions or permanent adaptation after programme support.
labour.distribution: Treatment and prior/network payout experiences differ; greater input spending is not by itself a measured gain for every household member.
labour.evidence_limit: No full-cost insurance-market viability, general constraint ranking, guaranteed profit benefit or universal psychological explanation follows.

title: Cooking systems: Odisha biomass stoves and a distinct supported LPG trial
period: Odisha: starting 2006–2007, up to four-year follow-up; HAPIN: randomisation 2018–2020 and pregnancy follow-up
summary: The Odisha programme's initial exposure gain fades as real cooking and maintenance mediate performance. HAPIN achieves high adherence and lower exposure under free ongoing support but no statistically significant birth-weight increase, distinguishing equipment, use, exposure and health links.

stages.invention: Neither study establishes an invention first; each tests a specified delivered configuration.
stages.feasibility: Laboratory promise is distinct from long-run programme performance. Odisha measures real use over years; HAPIN supplies equipment plus recurring fuel and support.
stages.deployment: Odisha uses phased random assignment across 44 villages/2,651 households. HAPIN randomises eligible pregnant women at selected four-country sites.
stages.diffusion: Neither supported trial establishes market diffusion. Older-stove use persists in Odisha; HAPIN reports high adherence during provision.
stages.scaling: Maintenance, delivery and recurring fuel costs are system components; the trials do not evaluate universal affordable rollout.
stages.non-adoption: Odisha ownership does not guarantee consistent use or repair; constraints cannot be inferred as ignorance. HAPIN's free-fuel context limits willingness-to-pay inference.
stages.displacement: Mixed use/stacking differs from effective biomass displacement. HAPIN's lower exposure does not imply an effect on every health endpoint.

counterevidence: The trials differ in technology, populations, dates, subsidy and outcomes, so they are not head-to-head product tests. HAPIN's null birth-weight result cannot simply inherit Odisha's low-use explanation.

episode.technology_configuration: A: inexpensive improved biomass stove with training and household responsibility for operation/maintenance in Odisha. B: LPG stove plus free continuing home-delivered fuel, instruction and adherence support in HAPIN.
episode.task: Cook everyday meals while reducing harmful exposure; fuel/time savings and particular health outcomes require separate measurements.
episode.population: A: 2,651 households in 44 Odisha villages, with primary cooks' outcomes. B: eligible pregnant women and households in selected sites in Guatemala, India, Peru and Rwanda. The populations and clinical endpoints are not interchangeable.
episode.interval: A: phased programme starting 2006–2007 and followed up to four years. B: randomisation from May 2018 to February 2020 with pregnancy/birth follow-up in the 2022 report.
contemporary_alternatives: Continued traditional biomass cooking
Mixed use of older and improved stoves
Supported LPG during HAPIN
Other commercial cooking systems not directly compared in either experiment
episode.adoption_measure: A: randomised offer, reported/observed use and maintenance, personal CO exposure, fuel/time and health outcomes. B: randomised package, adherence, personal particulate exposure and birth weight. Ownership is distinct from use; clinical endpoints differ.
episode.observation_limits: Odisha's full 2012 working paper and final 2016 abstract are separate editions of one experiment. HAPIN's free support and specific pregnant population limit transfer to commercial demand; this contribution inspects one HAPIN outcome paper only.

actors.chooser: Programmes select devices and support; households/cooks decide daily use within fuel, meal and family constraints. Trial assignment is not a household preference vote.
actors.payer: Odisha's programme and household contributions/support differ from HAPIN's free stove and continuing fuel provision; household time and repair costs remain real costs. No unified cost-effectiveness comparison is made.
actors.operator_maintainer: Primary cooks operate devices, typically within unpaid household work. Odisha households undertake upkeep/repair; HAPIN staff provide recurring fuel and adherence support.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Other household members and children exposed to cooking pollution, and fetuses in HAPIN's birth-weight outcome; primary cooks need not control every purchase or fuel decision.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Observed continued older-stove use shows some daily choice, while resource and meal constraints can limit options. HAPIN high adherence under support is not proof of unconstrained commercial willingness to pay.

labour.tasks: Cooking, fuel acquisition/handling, cleaning, chimney/device upkeep and repair; Odisha records additional repair time and does not realise expected fuel savings.
labour.entry_barriers: Suitable device and pots/meals, fuel access, recurring affordability, maintenance and instruction; the precise importance of each component was not separately randomised.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Cooks bear operation and exposure burdens but may not control purchases or cash. The studies do not fully identify intra-household bargaining effects.
labour.transition: Odisha follows operation up to four years; HAPIN follows a supported pregnancy intervention. Neither tracks permanent occupation or livelihood changes after full support ends.
labour.distribution: Primary cooks' exposure, household repair time and infant birth weight are distinct outcomes; a null in one does not establish equal effects for all people or all health outcomes.
labour.evidence_limit: No universal time-saving, health, fuel-saving or market-demand claim, and no head-to-head causal estimate of biomass versus LPG devices alone.

title: United States appliances and household production time
period: 1900–2005, with Cowan's strongest historical focus on the early twentieth century
summary: Attended machinery, changing output standards and domestic service complicate a simple device-to-hours story. Ramey's reconstructed time series records declining women's and increasing men's home-production time, but neither source identifies a particular appliance's causal contribution.

stages.invention: No first-invention claim; the case concerns operating appliances and household allocation.
stages.feasibility: Machines perform specified operations while handling/attendance may remain. Reduced physical exertion and unattended operation are different properties.
stages.deployment: Cowan documents appliances and domestic routines mainly through middle-class magazines and contemporary investigations.
stages.diffusion: Neither selected source provides an appliance-by-appliance ownership/use diffusion curve for the full 1900–2005 population.
stages.scaling: Utilities, income, service markets and standards can change alongside equipment; their separate effects are not estimated here.
stages.non-adoption: Manual work, hired help and purchased goods remain contemporary alternatives, with access varying by household.
stages.displacement: Particular operations and domestic-service arrangements change, but persistence of housework is not proof that machines had no value or that output was fixed.

counterevidence: Historical documentary populations are selective, and early time series require extrapolation. Some devices can directly save task time, but aggregate hours cannot isolate their effect or the distribution of gains.

episode.technology_configuration: Household appliances within changing domestic-service, utility and consumption arrangements; a broad historical bundle rather than a single assigned device.
episode.task: Produce household services such as cleaning, laundry, meals and care, with quantities/standards and paid outsourcing allowed to change.
episode.population: Cowan: mainly middle-class US magazine readership and households represented in contemporary investigations. Ramey: reconstructed national time-use groups, including women and men aged 18–64 and broader populations for aggregate comparisons.
episode.interval: Cowan emphasises early twentieth-century changes, especially the 1920s; Ramey's inspected series spans 1900–2005 with heterogeneous pre-1965 evidence and more representative later surveys.
contemporary_alternatives: Manual performance at home
Hired domestic labour or external laundry/services
Purchased household goods and prepared outputs
Different standards, quantities or division of household work
episode.adoption_measure: Historical descriptions of machine use plus reconstructed weekly home-production hours. Exact values in AGR-K22 refer to women aged 18–64; hours are neither device ownership nor a causal appliance effect.
episode.observation_limits: Magazines/advertisements are not universal practice. Early time diaries/tabulations require harmonisation and extrapolation, with simultaneous care and service quality difficult to compare. Source traditions may overlap.

actors.chooser: Households and purchasers choose appliances and service mixes, with gendered norms and control of income affecting who decides; advertisers influence claims but do not demonstrate actual preference change.
actors.payer: Household resources finance purchases, utilities and hired help; unpaid operators bear time/effort that purchase prices omit.
actors.operator_maintainer: Household members, especially women in the historical account, and paid domestic/service workers; attendance, handling and maintenance can persist with machines.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Household members receiving services, women doing unpaid work and domestic workers whose employment/tasks change; purchase consent and control are not measured uniformly.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Access to utilities, money, hired help and alternative labour allocation varies. Norms and household authority constrain practical choices; a purchase or persistent work pattern alone does not measure freely chosen preferences.

labour.tasks: Some physical operations become mechanical while handling, care, standards and household management change; work can shift between paid servants and unpaid family members.
labour.entry_barriers: Money, utilities, housing space and operating knowledge for appliance use; class and gender affect available alternatives and paid-work options.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Ownership of a device does not establish control over time saved or output standards. The selected sources do not isolate bargaining effects on employment.
labour.transition: Long-run group time trends are not individual career trajectories. Cowan's historical account traces reorganisation without a complete displaced-domestic-worker panel.
labour.distribution: Ramey estimates decreasing women's and increasing men's home-production hours; population-weighted totals depend on age/composition. Strenuousness and output quality are not measured by hours alone.
labour.evidence_limit: No appliance-specific causal effect on women's employment, automatic hours-liberation claim or national welfare estimate from these two sources.
